newsitem.title: FRANCE: Environmentalists begin fast at French N-plant.
newsitem.headline: Environmentalists begin fast at French N-plant.

text.p: About 40 environmentalists began a 48-hour fast on Thursday outside a fault-prone fast-breeder nuclear reactor in southeast France that the government has promised to close.

The fast is a prelude to a rally on Saturday to mark the 20th anniversary of a protest by about 60,000 anti-nuclear activists at the Superphenix plant during which a teacher died and hundreds of people were injured in clashes with police.
Relatives of the late physics teacher were among the 40 taking part in the fast in the Alpine town of Grenoble.

Since the controversial 1,200 megawatt Superphenix reactor started up in 1977, it has been plagued by faults and has only fed the electricity grid for only 10 months despite being on line for three times as long.
Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, who has described the 60 billion franc ($10.5 billion) reactor as too costly and of doubtful value, said last month he would close the reactor.
The fast breeder reactor, designed to produce more plutonium than it consumes, has been the bete noir of environmentalists for 20 years. One pressure group called it a dangerous dinosaur.
The former centre-right government had downgraded the reactor in 1994 to work at reduced power in order to study nuclear waste disposal.
Thursday's fast triggered a counter-protest by pro-nuclear supporters of the plant.
They set up a loudspeaker to blare out the praises of the nuclear industry, and denounced the planned attendance of some Environment Ministry officials at Saturday's rally.
Three quarters of France's electricity is generated by nuclear plants.
Environment Minister Dominique Voynet wrote regretting she was unable to come to Saturday's planned rally.
Voynet, who was the leader of the Green Party before the left's victory in the June elections, had earlier described the plant as a "stupid financial waste".
The reactor is 51 percent owned by Electricite de France, with Italy's ENEL and a Dutch-German-Belgium consortium as partners.
